text: Elizabeth J. Magie Phillips (née Magie; May 9, 1866 – March 2, 1948) was an American game designer, writer, feminist, and Georgist who invented The Landlord's Game, the precursor to Monopoly, to illustrate the economic teachings of progressive era economist Henry George. Born in Macomb, Illinois, in 1866 to Mary Jane (née Ritchie) and James K. Magie, a newspaper publisher and abolitionist who accompanied Abraham Lincoln in the late 1850s, Magie moved to the D.C. and Maryland area in the early 1880s, where she worked as a stenographer and typist at the Dead Letter Office. She was also a short story writer, poet, comedian, stage actress, feminist, and engineer. At age 26, she received a patent for an invention that improved the typewriting process by allowing paper to pass through rollers more easily; at that time, women held less than one percent of all patents. She briefly worked as a news reporter in the early 1900s and married Albert Wallace Phillips in 1910 at age 44; they had no children. Magie was an outspoken advocate for feminism and Georgism, an economic theory advocating a universal land tax based on land's usefulness, size, and location (the "single tax"), with surplus funds distributed to the public, which aimed to eliminate landowner power, promote land cultivation, and redistribute wealth to low-income individuals. This belief formed the foundation of The Landlord's Game. She believed women were as capable as men in invention and business, a view considered novel and radical in the 1800s; as a stenographer, she earned about $10 a week, insufficient to support herself without a husband. To highlight women's and Black people's subjugated status, she published an advertisement auctioning herself as a "young woman American slave" seeking a husband, which sparked national attention and established her as a bold feminist. In 1903, she applied for a patent on The Landlord's Game, which was granted U.S. Patent 748,626 on January 5, 1904—before women gained national voting rights. The game was designed to demonstrate the negative effects of land monopolism and the benefits of a land value tax, featuring two settings: a monopolist version (Monopoly) where players aim to own industries and drive others out, and an anti-monopolist version (Prosperity) where players create products and interact with opponents. In 1906, she moved to Chicago and co-founded the Economic Game Co. with fellow Georgists to self-publish the game. In 1910, Parker Brothers published her humorous card game Mock Trial. The Newbie Game Co. in Scotland patented a version called "Bre'r Fox and Bre'r Rabbit," though no evidence confirms British patent protection. In 1924, after her original patent expired in 1921, she and her husband patented a revised edition of the game to regain control as it was being copied at colleges. In 1932, the Adgame Company of Washington, D.C. published her second edition, which included both Monopoly and Prosperity. She also developed Bargain Day (1937), a department store-themed game, and King's Men (1937), an abstract strategy game, as well as a third version of The Landlord's Game in 1939. Magie died at age 81 in 1948 and was buried with her husband Albert Wallace Phillips, who died in 1937, in Columbia Gardens Cemetery, Arlington, Virginia. She had no children and was not credited during her lifetime for her impact on board games or American culture. The game gained popularity among college students at Harvard, Columbia, and the University of Pennsylvania, as well as left-leaning middle-class families and Quakers in the Northeast. Thirty years after its invention in 1904, Parker Brothers released a modified version known as Monopoly, which Charles Darrow claimed to have invented in his basement. Magie publicly criticized Darrow and reported earning only $500 from her invention and receiving no credit. In a 1936 Washington, D.C. newspaper interview, she expressed her frustration over the similarities between Monopoly and The Landlord's Game and the lack of recognition and financial return. After Ralph Anspach, creator of the Anti-Monopoly game, discovered Magie's patents during a legal dispute with Parker Brothers, her contributions gained renewed attention. Despite Darrow and Parker Brothers claiming ownership, Magie has posthumously received credit for one of the most popular board games. Her game introduced the circular board format, a novel departure from linear games of the time, and provided entertainment that taught about Georgist principles, wealth distribution, and the dangers of monopolies—elements absent from Darrow’s version of Monopoly. Magie also contributed to the women's movement and Black people's rights by publishing political material in newspapers and inventing games during a period when women held less than one percent of U.S. patents.
